quiz.explain: Multiplying (3, 4, 5) by 2, 3, 4, ... gives a new triple every time, and that never ends.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only the few famous triples exist

teach.ask: Gappu asks: How do I check if 5, 12, 13 is a Pythagorean triple?
teach.praise: 25 + 144 = 169 = 13². The two small squares add up to the big square. It is a triple!
teach.nudge: What do you do with 5 and 12? Then what do you compare the answer with?

topics.title: Proof ideas and using the converse

learn.hook: Can you prove a² + b² = c² with just four paper triangles and a square? Yes, with a cut-and-arrange trick!
points: Area proof: draw a big square of side (a + b). Put 4 copies of the right triangle in its corners. The space left in the middle is a tilted square of side c.
Big square area = 4 triangles + middle square: (a + b)² = 4 × ½ab + c². So a² + 2ab + b² = 2ab + c², which gives a² + b² = c².
Rearrangement: slide the same 4 triangles into a different position in the big square, and the space left is two squares, a² and b². Same leftover area, so a² + b² = c².
Baudhayana used the diagonal to double a square: the square on the diagonal of a square has twice its area.
Converse in action: if the longest side c gives a² + b² = c², the triangle is right-angled. If a² + b² > c² it is acute; if a² + b² < c² it is obtuse.

example.q: Use the area proof with a = 3 and b = 4 to find c.

learn.reallife: Masons mark a perfect right angle for a house corner with a knotted rope stretched into a 3-4-5 triangle.

Place four copies of the right triangle in its corners

A triangle with sides 4, 5 and 6 has a right angle.
16 + 25 = 41, but 6² = 36. It is an acute triangle.
The diagonal of a square with side 1 has length √2.
In every triangle, a² + b² = c².
This is true only for right triangles.
A knotted rope with sides 3, 4 and 5 units can be used to mark a right angle.
3² + 4² = 5², so by the converse the angle between 3 and 4 is 90°.
If both legs of a right triangle are doubled, the hypotenuse also doubles.

quiz.q: In the area proof, a big square of side (a + b) holds 4 right triangles with legs a and b, and a middle square of side c. If a = 3 and b = 4, what is the area of the middle square?
quiz.explain: Big square = 7² = 49. Four triangles = 4 × 6 = 24. Middle square = 49 − 24 = 25, so c = 5.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract the triangles, or uses only one triangle

quiz.q: A triangle has sides 5 cm, 6 cm and 8 cm. What kind of triangle is it?
quiz.explain: 5² + 6² = 61, which is less than 8² = 64. When the two smaller squares add to less than the largest square, the triangle is obtuse.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any triangle with whole-number sides is right-angled

quiz.q: What is the diagonal of a square of side 5 cm? (Use √2 ≈ 1.41.)
quiz.mistake: Adds the two sides (10 cm) instead of using the theorem

quiz.q: Baudhayana's idea: a square is drawn on the diagonal of a square of side 6 cm. What is the area of the new square?
quiz.explain: Diagonal² = 6² + 6² = 72. The new square's area is diagonal², which is 72 cm², twice the original 36 cm².
quiz.mistake: Doubles the side (12 cm), which makes 144 cm², four times the area

quiz.q: Why do masons use a knotted rope with sides 3, 4 and 5 units?
options: Because 3² + 4² = 5², so the triangle has a right angle for making square corners
Because it makes an equilateral triangle
Because ropes cannot make other shapes
quiz.explain: By the converse of the theorem, sides 3, 4, 5 must make a right angle between the 3 and 4 sides.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the converse of the theorem to real right angles

quiz.q: A triangle has sides 9, 10 and 12. Is it acute, right or obtuse?
quiz.explain: 9² + 10² = 181, which is more than 12² = 144. When the two smaller squares add to more than the largest, all angles are acute.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up which way the inequality points to acute or obtuse

quiz.q: A right triangle has legs 5 and 12. If both legs are doubled, what is the new hypotenuse?
quiz.explain: The old hypotenuse is 13. Doubling both legs doubles the hypotenuse: 26. Check: 10² + 24² = 676 = 26².
quiz.mistake: Thinks the hypotenuse stays the same or becomes 4 times bigger

quiz.q: In the rearrangement proof, the four triangles are moved inside the same big square so that two squares are left uncovered. What are their areas?
quiz.explain: The leftover space is a square of side a and a square of side b. Before the move it was one square of side c, so a² + b² = c².
quiz.mistake: Confuses the triangles' areas (½ab) with the leftover squares

teach.ask: Gappu asks: How does putting 4 triangles inside a big square prove a² + b² = c²?
teach.praise: The leftover space is c² in one arrangement and a² + b² in the other. Same space, so they are equal. Mind blown!
teach.nudge: What is left uncovered in the middle? And what is left after you move the triangles?

learn.hook: One samosa costs ₹15, two cost ₹30, ten cost ₹150. Double the samosas and you double the bill. That is direct proportion!
points: Two quantities are in direct proportion if, when one is multiplied by a number, the other is multiplied by the same number.
In direct proportion, y ÷ x stays the same. We can write y = kx, where k is the constant.
Examples: number of pens and their cost; petrol used and distance at a steady speed; time and pay for a fixed hourly wage.
Test a table: divide each y by its x. If you always get the same number, it is direct proportion.
Not everything that grows together is in proportion. A child's age and height both grow, but height does not double when age doubles.

example.q: 5 m of cloth costs ₹350. What is the cost of 8 m?
steps: Cost ÷ length stays the same: 350 ÷ 5 = ₹70 per metre

learn.reallife: Your phone data bill, petrol pump meters and auto-rickshaw fares (after the minimum charge) grow in direct proportion.

quiz.mistake: Multiplies 270 by 6 instead of dividing

learn.hook: One painter takes 12 days to paint a house. Do 3 painters also take 12 days? No, just 4 days! More hands, fewer days.
points: Two quantities are in inverse proportion if, when one is multiplied by a number, the other is divided by the same number.
In inverse proportion, x × y stays the same.
Examples: workers and days for a fixed job; speed and time for a fixed distance; number of children and laddoos each gets from a fixed box.
To solve: find the fixed product first, then divide by the new value.
Not every 'one goes up, other goes down' is inverse proportion. Check that the product stays the same.

learn.hook: The Vande Bharat Express can run at 160 km/h. A cheetah can sprint at over 100 km/h, but only for a few seconds. Who wins a long race? Rates tell the story!
points: A rate compares two different kinds of quantities: km per hour, ₹ per kg, words per minute, heartbeats per minute.
A unit rate is the amount for 1 unit: 300 km in 5 hours is 60 km per hour.
Speed = distance ÷ time, distance = speed × time, time = distance ÷ speed.
To change km/h to m/s, multiply by 1000/3600 = 5/18. So 72 km/h = 20 m/s.
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. It is not always the average of the two speeds.

example.q: A train goes 180 km in 2 hours and then 120 km in 2 hours. What is its average speed?

learn.reallife: Cricket commentators give run rates per over, doctors check pulse rate per minute, and shops show price per kg.

learn.hook: With just a pencil, a ruler and a compass you can draw a perfect 60°, 30°, 90° or 45° angle, without ever looking at a protractor!
points: A compass keeps a fixed distance, so every point on an arc is the same distance from the compass point.
Perpendicular bisector of AB: draw arcs of the same radius (more than half of AB) from A and from B. Join the two points where they cross. Every point on this line is equally far from A and B.
Angle bisector: draw an arc from the vertex cutting both arms. From those two points draw equal arcs that cross. Join the crossing point to the vertex.
60°: draw an arc from the vertex, then an arc of the same radius from where it cuts the arm. This makes an equilateral triangle. Bisect 60° to get 30°; bisect 90° to get 45°.
A triangle can be drawn from three sides only if any two sides together are longer than the third.

example.q: How can you construct an angle of 45° with a ruler and compass?
steps: Draw a line and mark a point O on it
Construct a perpendicular at O to get 90°

learn.reallife: Architects, carpenters and rangoli artists use compass constructions to get exact angles and symmetric designs.

pairs: arc from vertex, same arc from where it cuts the arm
draw a perpendicular to a line

games.title: Compass check
items: Every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is the same distance from A and from B.
That is exactly what makes it the perpendicular bisector.
For a perpendicular bisector, the arcs must have a radius less than half of AB.
With less than half, the arcs from A and B would not meet. The radius must be more than half.
A triangle can be drawn with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm.
3 + 4 = 7, which is less than 8, so the sides cannot meet.
Bisecting 90° and then bisecting one half again gives 22.5°.
An angle bisector divides an angle into two equal parts.
Bisect means cut into two equal halves.

quiz.q: What angle do you get when you bisect a 90° angle?
quiz.explain: Bisecting cuts an angle into two equal halves: 90° ÷ 2 = 45°.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the angle instead of halving it

quiz.q: Riya draws arcs of the same radius from points A and B and joins the two points where the arcs cross. What has she drawn?
quiz.explain: The two crossing points are each equally far from A and B. The line through them cuts AB in half at 90°.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the perpendicular bisector with the angle bisector

quiz.q: Point P lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB, and PA = 7 cm. What is PB?

quiz.explain: 5 + 6 = 11 is more than 10, so the sides can meet. In the others, the two shorter sides add up to the longest side or less.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any three lengths can make a triangle

quiz.q: To construct 60°, you draw an arc from the vertex and then an arc of the same radius from where it cuts the arm. Why does this give 60°?
options: It makes an equilateral triangle, and each angle of that triangle is 60°
quiz.explain: The vertex, the first cut point and the crossing point are all one radius apart, forming an equilateral triangle. Each of its angles is 180° ÷ 3 = 60°.
quiz.mistake: Follows the steps without seeing the equilateral triangle behind them

quiz.q: Kabir bisects an angle of 130°. What is the size of each part?
quiz.explain: Bisecting means halving: 130° ÷ 2 = 65°.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the angle

quiz.q: Which construction gives an angle of 120°?
options: Make two 60° angles side by side
quiz.explain: 60° + 60° = 120°. Bisecting 60° gives 30°, bisecting 90° gives 45°, and a perpendicular gives 90°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks bisecting makes an angle bigger

quiz.q: Aisha bisects a 60° angle, then bisects one of the halves. What angle does she get?
quiz.mistake: Stops after the first bisection

teach.ask: Gappu asks: I have lost my protractor! How can I still draw a 30° angle?
teach.praise: Make 60° with compass arcs (an equilateral triangle), then bisect it to get 30°. No protractor needed!
teach.nudge: Which angle can you make easily with just a compass? How do you get half of it?

topics.title: Faces, edges, vertices and Euler's formula

learn.hook: Count the faces, corners and edges of any box, add the faces and corners, then subtract the edges. You will always get 2. Try it on a dice!
points: A solid's flat surfaces are faces, the lines where two faces meet are edges, and the corners are vertices.
A cube or cuboid has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. A square pyramid has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices.
A polyhedron is a solid whose faces are all flat polygons. Cylinders, cones and spheres have curved surfaces, so they are not polyhedra.
Euler's formula for polyhedra: F + V − E = 2. For a cube: 6 + 8 − 12 = 2.
A prism has two identical ends joined by rectangles. A pyramid has one base with triangles meeting at the top.

example.q: A pentagonal prism has 7 faces and 15 edges. How many vertices does it have?

learn.reallife: Gift boxes, tents, the pyramid-shaped roof of a temple and a cricket ball show the difference between polyhedra and curved solids.

quiz.q: How many edges does a cube have?
quiz.explain: A cube has 4 edges on the top, 4 on the bottom and 4 upright ones: 12 edges.
quiz.mistake: Counts faces (6) or vertices (8) instead of edges

quiz.q: A polyhedron has 8 faces and 6 vertices. How many edges does it have? (Use F + V − E = 2.)
quiz.mistake: Adds 2 instead of subtracting it

quiz.q: How many vertices does a square pyramid have?
quiz.explain: It has 4 corners at the square base and 1 at the top: 5 vertices.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the top point (apex)

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a polyhedron?
quiz.explain: A cylinder has curved surfaces. A polyhedron must have only flat polygon faces.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any solid shape is a polyhedron

quiz.q: A triangular prism has 5 faces and 6 vertices. How many edges does it have?
quiz.explain: F + V − E = 2 gives 5 + 6 − E = 2, so E = 9. Count check: 3 + 3 edges on the triangles and 3 joining them.
quiz.mistake: Adds F and V without subtracting 2

quiz.q: Meena wraps a cuboid-shaped gift box, covering every face. How many faces does she cover?
quiz.explain: A cuboid has 6 faces: top, bottom, front, back, left and right.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the side faces, or counts corners

quiz.q: A pentagonal prism has 7 faces and 15 edges. How many vertices does it have?
quiz.explain: 7 + V − 15 = 2, so V = 10. Each pentagon end has 5 corners: 5 + 5 = 10.
quiz.mistake: Gets the signs in Euler's formula mixed up

quiz.q: Can a polyhedron have 10 faces, 10 vertices and 15 edges?
options: No, because F + V − E would be 5, not 2
No, because 15 is an odd number
quiz.explain: Every polyhedron obeys F + V − E = 2. Here 10 + 10 − 15 = 5, so no such polyhedron exists.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the number of edges must be even (a triangular prism has 9)

teach.ask: Gappu asks: What is Euler's formula, and how can I check it on a cube?
teach.praise: Faces plus vertices minus edges is 2. For a cube: 6 + 8 − 12 = 2. Euler was a genius, and so are you!
teach.nudge: Which three things do you count on a cube? What do you do with them?

learn.hook: Hold a glass at eye level: it looks like a rectangle. Look down into it from above: it is a circle! Same glass, different views.
points: A solid can look different from the front, the side and the top. The top view is also called the plan.
A cylinder standing up: rectangle from the front, circle from the top. A cone on its base: triangle from the front, circle from the top. A sphere looks like a circle from every side.
A cube looks like a square from the front, side and top.
For stacks of cubes, count layer by layer. The top view shows how many columns there are.
A net is a flat pattern that folds into a solid. Cylinder: a rectangle and 2 circles. Cone: a curved sector and a circle. Square pyramid: a square and 4 triangles. Cube: 6 squares.

example.q: Arjun puts 3 cubes in a row on the floor and 1 cube on top of the middle one. Describe the front view and count the cubes.
steps: Bottom row: 3 squares side by side
Top: 1 square above the middle one
example.answer: Front view: 3 squares with 1 on top of the middle; 4 cubes

learn.reallife: Architects draw front, side and top views of buildings, and sweet-box makers cut flat nets that fold into boxes.

games.title: Top view: circle or not?
buckets: Top view is not a circle
items: Triangular prism lying on a rectangular face

quiz.q: What does an upright cylinder look like from the top?
quiz.explain: Looking down, you see only the round top face, so the top view is a circle.
quiz.mistake: Gives the front view (rectangle) instead of the top view

quiz.q: What is the front view of a cone standing on its base?
quiz.explain: From the front, the cone narrows from a wide base to a point, so it looks like a triangle.
quiz.mistake: Gives the top view (circle) instead of the front view

quiz.q: Which solid looks like a circle from the front, the side and the top?
quiz.explain: A sphere is round in every direction, so every view is a circle.
quiz.mistake: Picks cylinder, whose front view is a rectangle

quiz.q: Arjun stacks cubes: 3 in a row on the floor and 1 on top of the middle one. How many cubes does he use?
quiz.explain: 3 cubes in the bottom row and 1 on top: 3 + 1 = 4.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the bottom layer

quiz.q: Which net folds into a cylinder?
options: A circle and a curved sector
quiz.explain: The rectangle rolls into the curved side, and the two circles become the top and bottom. A circle and a sector make a cone.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the cylinder's net with the cone's net

quiz.q: Which shapes make up the net of a square pyramid?
quiz.explain: The square is the base, and the 4 triangles fold up to meet at the top.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the pyramid with a prism or cube

quiz.q: A cube with edge 3 cm is unfolded into a net of 6 squares. What is the total area of the net?
quiz.explain: Each square is 3 × 3 = 9 cm². Six squares: 6 × 9 = 54 cm².
quiz.mistake: Finds the volume (27) or uses only 4 faces (36)

quiz.q: Joseph builds a 2 × 2 × 2 cube from small cubes. How many small cubes can he see from directly above?
quiz.explain: From the top you see only the top layer, which is 2 × 2 = 4 small cubes. The bottom 4 are hidden.
quiz.mistake: Counts all 8 cubes, including hidden ones

teach.ask: Gappu asks: Why does my cylinder-shaped water bottle look like a rectangle sometimes and a circle at other times?
teach.praise: From the front it looks like a rectangle, and from the top it looks like a circle. It depends on the view! Clever!
teach.nudge: Where are you looking from when it looks like a circle? And when it looks like a rectangle?

learn.hook: Kabir scored 12, 30, 45, 30 and 8 runs in five matches. Is he a 30-run batter or a 25-run batter? It depends on which 'average' you use!
points: Data are facts or numbers we collect. Putting them in order or in a table makes them easier to read.
Mean (the usual average) = sum of all values ÷ number of values.
Median = the middle value after arranging the data in order. If there are two middle values, take their mean.
Mode = the value that appears most often.
Range = largest value − smallest value. It tells how spread out the data are.

example.q: Kabir's runs: 12, 30, 45, 30, 8. Find the mean, median, mode and range.

learn.reallife: Cricket averages, your class's average marks, and the most popular size of school shoes all come from these ideas.

quiz.q: Kabir's scores in 5 matches are 12, 30, 45, 30 and 8. What is his mean score?
quiz.explain: Sum = 125 and there are 5 matches, so the mean is 125 ÷ 5 = 25.
quiz.mistake: Gives the total (125) or the most common score (30)

quiz.q: What is the median of 12, 30, 45, 30, 8?
quiz.explain: In order: 8, 12, 30, 30, 45. The middle (3rd) value is 30.
quiz.mistake: Picks the middle value without arranging in order (45)

quiz.q: The heights of 6 plants are 10, 14, 15, 18, 20 and 25 cm. What is the median height?
quiz.explain: With 6 values, the two middle ones are 15 and 18. Median = (15 + 18) ÷ 2 = 16.5 cm.
quiz.mistake: Picks one of the two middle values, or finds the mean (17)

quiz.q: Shoe sizes in a group: 5, 6, 6, 7, 6, 8, 5, 6. What is the mode?
quiz.explain: Size 6 appears 4 times, more than any other size.
quiz.mistake: Picks the largest value, or the first value in the list

quiz.q: The mean of 4 numbers is 15. Three of them are 10, 12 and 20. What is the fourth number?
quiz.explain: Total of all 4 numbers = 4 × 15 = 60. The three known numbers add to 42, so the fourth is 60 − 42 = 18.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the missing number must equal the mean (15)

quiz.q: The midday temperatures (in °C) for a week were 31, 34, 29, 35, 33, 30 and 32. What is the range in °C?
quiz.explain: Range = highest − lowest = 35 − 29 = 6.
quiz.mistake: Gives the highest value or the median instead of the spread

quiz.q: Which measure is best for finding the most popular ice-cream flavour in a class?
quiz.explain: Flavours are names, not numbers, so we cannot add or order them. The mode tells which flavour was chosen most often.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the mean is always the right average

quiz.q: Riya's mean mark in 6 tests is 70. After a 7th test her mean becomes 72. What did she score in the 7th test?
quiz.explain: Total for 6 tests = 6 × 70 = 420. Total for 7 tests = 7 × 72 = 504. So the 7th test = 504 − 420 = 84.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the new mark is just the new mean, or adds the two means

teach.ask: Gappu asks: How do I find the median of 9, 2, 7, 4, 5?
teach.praise: Put them in order: 2, 4, 5, 7, 9. The middle one is 5. That is the median!
teach.nudge: What must you do to the numbers first? Then which one do you pick?

topics.title: Bar graphs, dot plots and pie charts

learn.hook: A picture can tell a story faster than a long table. One glance at a graph and you know who won the class election!
points: A bar graph uses bars of equal width with gaps between them. The height (or length) shows the value.
A double bar graph puts two bars side by side for each category, for example boys and girls.
A dot plot puts one dot for every value above a number line, so clusters and gaps are easy to spot.
Always read the scale: if 1 unit = 5 students, a bar 4 units tall shows 20 students. The scale should start at 0.
A pie chart shows parts of a whole as slices. Slice angle = (part ÷ whole) × 360°.

example.q: In a survey of 120 students, 30 like cricket best. What angle should the cricket slice have in a pie chart?

learn.reallife: News channels show election results as bar graphs and pie charts, and sports apps show runs per over as bars.

items.text: If 1 unit = 5 students, a bar 6 units tall shows ___ students
A slice that is 1/4 of a pie chart has an angle of ___
In a dot plot, each dot stands for one data ___
All the slices of a pie chart add up to ___

games.title: Graph facts
items: In a bar graph, the width of a bar shows its value.
All bars have the same width. The height (or length) shows the value.
A dot plot shows every single data value.
There is one dot for each value.
In a pie chart, a 180° slice shows half of the data.
The scale on a bar graph should start at 0 so that bar heights can be compared fairly.
If the scale starts higher, small differences look huge.
A double bar graph can compare two groups side by side.
Two bars for each category make comparing easy.
If 1 unit = 10 runs, a bar 3.5 units tall shows 3.5 runs.

quiz.q: A bar graph shows books read in a class library: Mon 4, Tue 7, Wed 3, Thu 6. On which day were the most books read?
quiz.explain: Tuesday's bar is the tallest, at 7 books.
quiz.mistake: Picks the last bar or the first bar instead of the tallest

quiz.q: Books read: Mon 4, Tue 7, Wed 3, Thu 6. How many more books were read on Tuesday than on Wednesday?
quiz.explain: Tuesday 7 − Wednesday 3 = 4 more books.
quiz.mistake: Adds the two values instead of finding the difference

quiz.q: On a bar graph, 1 unit stands for 50 trees. A bar is 7 units tall. How many trees does it show?
quiz.explain: Each unit is 50 trees, so 7 units = 7 × 50 = 350 trees.
quiz.mistake: Reads the bar height without using the scale

quiz.q: In a class of 40, 10 students walk to school. What angle should the 'walk' slice have in a pie chart?
quiz.explain: 10 out of 40 is 1/4 of the class. 1/4 × 360° = 90°.
quiz.mistake: Uses the number of students as the angle

quiz.q: A dot plot shows goals scored by a team in its matches: 0 goals (3 dots), 1 goal (5 dots), 2 goals (2 dots), 3 goals (1 dot). How many matches did the team play?
quiz.explain: Each dot is one match. 3 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 11 matches.
quiz.mistake: Counts the number of columns (4) instead of the dots

quiz.q: Same dot plot: 0 goals (3 dots), 1 goal (5 dots), 2 goals (2 dots), 3 goals (1 dot). How many goals did the team score in all?
quiz.explain: Multiply goals by the number of matches: 0 × 3 + 1 × 5 + 2 × 2 + 3 × 1 = 0 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 12.
quiz.mistake: Counts the dots (matches) instead of the goals

quiz.q: Which graph is best for showing what share of the whole each part is, like how Meena spends her day?
quiz.explain: A pie chart shows parts of one whole as slices, so you see each part's share at a glance.
quiz.mistake: Uses a line graph, which shows change over time

quiz.q: A double bar graph shows the children who like each sport. Cricket: boys 12, girls 9. Kabaddi: boys 6, girls 8. How many children like kabaddi?
quiz.explain: Add both bars for kabaddi: 6 boys + 8 girls = 14 children.
quiz.mistake: Finds the difference between the bars, or adds the cricket bars

teach.ask: Gappu asks: A bar graph says 1 unit = 20 birds. A bar is 3 units tall. How many birds is that?
teach.praise: Each unit is 20 birds, so 3 × 20 = 60 birds. That is a big flock!
teach.nudge: What does one unit on the graph stand for? What do you do with the 3?

learn.hook: A doctor's fever chart, a share-market screen and your height on the door frame all tell stories of change. Line graphs show how things change over time.
points: A line graph plots points for values at different times and joins them with line segments.
Time usually goes on the horizontal axis and the quantity on the vertical axis.
A line going up shows an increase, going down shows a decrease, and a flat line shows no change.
A steeper line means a faster change.
In a distance–time graph, a straight sloping line means a steady speed; speed = distance ÷ time.

example.q: Temperatures: 6 am 18°C, 9 am 22°C, 12 noon 30°C, 3 pm 32°C, 6 pm 26°C. Between which two times did the temperature rise the most?
example.answer: Between 9 am and 12 noon (a rise of 8°)

learn.reallife: Weather reports, a patient's temperature chart and a city's population over the years are all shown as line graphs.

games.title: Line graph or bar graph?
buckets: Line graph is a good choice
Bar graph is a better choice
items: Your height every year from age 5 to 13
Temperature every hour of a day
Price of petrol each month for a year
Favourite fruits of students in a class
Number of students in each section of Class 8
Runs scored by each player in one match

items.text: A line that goes up from left to right shows an ___
A flat, horizontal part of a line graph shows ___
In a distance–time graph, a steeper line means a ___ speed
In a line graph over time, time is usually on the ___ axis

quiz.q: Temperatures: 6 am 18°C, 9 am 22°C, 12 noon 30°C, 3 pm 32°C, 6 pm 26°C. At which of these times was it hottest?
quiz.explain: The highest point on the graph is 32°C at 3 pm.
quiz.mistake: Assumes noon is always the hottest time

quiz.q: Using the same temperatures, by how many degrees did it rise from 9 am to 12 noon?
quiz.explain: 30 − 22 = 8 degrees.
quiz.mistake: Gives the reading at noon instead of the change

quiz.q: Using the same temperatures, between which two times did the temperature fall?
quiz.explain: From 32°C at 3 pm it went down to 26°C at 6 pm. All other parts go up.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a smaller rise with a fall

quiz.q: Harpreet's plant was 4 cm in week 1, 7 cm in week 2, 10 cm in week 3 and 13 cm in week 4. If it keeps growing the same way, how tall will it be in week 5?
quiz.explain: It grows 3 cm every week, so the line keeps the same steepness: 13 + 3 = 16 cm.
quiz.mistake: Adds 1 or doubles instead of continuing the steady +3 pattern

quiz.q: On a line graph, what does a horizontal (flat) part show?
options: The quantity did not change during that time
quiz.explain: If the line stays at the same height, the value stays the same for that time.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a flat line means the value dropped to zero

quiz.q: A cyclist's distance–time graph is a straight line from 0 km at 0 hours to 45 km at 3 hours. What is the speed in km/h?
quiz.explain: A straight line means steady speed. Speed = 45 km ÷ 3 h = 15 km/h.
quiz.mistake: Reads the final distance as the speed

quiz.q: Which data is best shown with a line graph?
options: Number of boys and girls in each class
Your weight every month for a year
Kinds of trees in a park
quiz.explain: Weight changes over time, and a line graph shows change over time. The others compare separate categories.
quiz.mistake: Uses a line graph for categories that have no order in time

quiz.q: Aisha's savings were ₹200 in January, ₹350 in February, ₹350 in March and ₹600 in April. During which period did her savings not change?
quiz.explain: Savings were ₹350 in both February and March, so the line is flat there.
quiz.mistake: Looks for the smallest bar instead of two equal readings

teach.ask: Gappu asks: How can I tell from a line graph when something is growing fastest?
teach.praise: Where the line goes up most steeply, the growth is fastest. I can read graphs now!
teach.nudge: Look at the different parts of the line. Which part climbs the most in the same time?

learn.hook: A pen costs ₹p and a notebook ₹n. Without knowing the prices, you can still write the bill for 3 pens and 2 notebooks: 3p + 2n. That is the power of algebra!
points: An algebraic expression uses numbers, letters (variables) and operations, like 3x + 5y − 2.
Terms are the parts joined by + or −. In the term −5y, the coefficient is −5.
Like terms have the same letters with the same powers: 3x² and −5x² are like terms, but 3x and 3x² are not.
We can add or subtract only like terms: 4a + 3b + 2a = 6a + 3b.
To evaluate an expression, put in (substitute) the value of each letter: if x = 3, then 2x² + 1 = 2 × 9 + 1 = 19.

example.q: Simplify (5x + 3y − 2) − (2x − y + 4).
steps: Remove the brackets; the minus changes every sign in the second bracket: 5x + 3y − 2 − 2x + y − 4

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers, coders and scientists all use letters to write rules that work for any number, like total cost = price × quantity.

quiz.q: Simplify 4a + 3b + 2a − b.
quiz.explain: Add like terms only: 4a + 2a = 6a and 3b − b = 2b.
quiz.mistake: Adds unlike terms together into one term

quiz.q: What is the coefficient of y in 7x − 5y + 3?
quiz.explain: The term with y is −5y, so its coefficient is −5. The sign belongs to the term.
quiz.mistake: Drops the minus sign in front of the term

quiz.q: Find the value of 2x² + 1 when x = 3.
quiz.explain: x² = 9, so 2 × 9 + 1 = 19. Square x first, then multiply by 2.
quiz.mistake: Squares 2x instead of x, getting (2 × 3)² + 1 = 37

quiz.q: Which pair are like terms?
quiz.explain: Like terms have exactly the same letters with the same powers. Both 3x² and −5x² have x².
quiz.mistake: Thinks terms with the same number in front are like terms

quiz.q: Simplify (5x + 3y − 2) − (2x − y + 4).
quiz.explain: Subtracting a bracket changes every sign inside it: 5x + 3y − 2 − 2x + y − 4 = 3x + 4y − 6.
quiz.mistake: Changes only the first sign inside the second bracket

quiz.q: A pen costs ₹p and a notebook costs ₹n. Riya buys 3 pens and 2 notebooks. Which expression gives the total cost in rupees?
quiz.explain: 3 pens cost 3 × p = 3p and 2 notebooks cost 2 × n = 2n. Total = 3p + 2n.
quiz.mistake: Combines unlike terms or swaps the numbers

quiz.q: If a = 2 and b = −3, what is a² − ab?
quiz.mistake: Forgets that subtracting a negative number means adding

quiz.q: How many terms are there in 3x² − 4xy + 7y − 9?
quiz.explain: The terms are 3x², −4xy, 7y and −9. That is 4 terms.
quiz.mistake: Does not count the number term −9, or counts letters

teach.ask: Gappu asks: Can I add 3x and 2y to get 5xy?
teach.praise: Only like terms can be added. 3x and 2y have different letters, so it stays 3x + 2y. Thanks!
teach.nudge: What must two terms have in common before we can add them?

learn.hook: Think of any number. Double it, add 10, halve it, then take away the number you first thought of. Your answer is 5! Algebra explains the magic.
points: Let the secret number be n and follow each step: 2n → 2n + 10 → n + 5 → 5. The n disappears, so everyone gets 5.
Patterns can be written as rules. 5, 8, 11, 14, ... goes up by 3 each time, so the nth term is 3n + 2.
Matchstick squares in a row use 4, 7, 10, ... sticks: 3n + 1 sticks for n squares.
Calendar trick: in any 2 × 2 block of dates with top-left n, the four dates are n, n + 1, n + 7, n + 8, which add to 4n + 16.
Check a rule by testing it with the first few terms.

example.q: Matchstick squares in a row need 4, 7, 10, ... sticks. How many sticks are needed for 20 squares?

learn.reallife: Magicians, puzzle makers and computer programmers use rules like 3n + 1 to predict what comes next.

items.text: The pattern 2, 4, 6, 8, ... has the rule ___
The pattern 1, 4, 9, 16, ... has the rule ___
The pattern 3, 5, 7, 9, ... has the rule ___
Think of n, add 3, then double. You get ___

quiz.q: Think of a number, double it, add 10, halve the result, then subtract the number you started with. What do you always get?
quiz.explain: With n: 2n, then 2n + 10, then n + 5, then n + 5 − n = 5.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that halving also halves the 10

quiz.q: Matchstick squares in a row use 4, 7, 10, ... sticks. How many sticks are needed for 20 squares?
quiz.explain: The rule is 3n + 1, so for 20 squares: 3 × 20 + 1 = 61. Neighbouring squares share a stick.
quiz.mistake: Uses 4 sticks for every square (80), forgetting that sticks are shared

quiz.q: What is the rule for the nth term of 5, 8, 11, 14, ...?
quiz.explain: The terms go up by 3, so the rule starts with 3n. For n = 1, 3n = 3, and we need 5, so add 2: 3n + 2.
quiz.mistake: Uses the first term (5) as the number added

quiz.q: On a calendar, Kabir picks a 2 × 2 block of dates whose top-left date is n. What is the sum of the four dates?
quiz.explain: The dates are n, n + 1 (next day), n + 7 (a week later) and n + 8. Sum = 4n + 16.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the date below is n + 1 instead of n + 7

quiz.q: Aisha says: think of a number, add 4, multiply by 3, then subtract 12. What is the answer always equal to?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies only n by 3 and forgets to multiply the 4

quiz.q: A pattern has the rule 4n − 1. What is its 10th term?
quiz.mistake: Adds 1 instead of subtracting

quiz.q: Which expression gives the sum of three consecutive numbers starting at n?
quiz.explain: The numbers are n, n + 1 and n + 2. Their sum is 3n + 3.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the +1 and +2, or adds 1 + 2 + 3

quiz.q: A pattern of triangles uses 3, 5, 7, 9, ... matchsticks (rule 2n + 1). Which term uses 51 matchsticks?
quiz.mistake: Puts 51 into the rule as n instead of solving for n

teach.ask: Gappu asks: Why does the 'double, add 10, halve, minus your number' trick always give 5?
teach.praise: Call the number n: 2n + 10, halved is n + 5, and taking away n leaves 5. The n cancels! Magic solved!
teach.nudge: What if you use a letter like n for the secret number? What happens to it at the end?

learn.hook: An equation is like a balanced weighing scale at the sabzi mandi. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other, and it stays balanced!
points: An equation says two expressions are equal. Solving it means finding the value of the letter that makes it true.
Keep the balance: add, subtract, multiply or divide both sides by the same number (never divide by 0).
Letters on both sides: move the letter terms to one side and the numbers to the other. 5x − 7 = 2x + 8 → 3x = 15 → x = 5.
Brackets: expand first. Fractions: multiply both sides by the LCM of the denominators.
Always check your answer by putting it back into the original equation.

example.q: Solve 5x − 7 = 2x + 8 and check.

learn.reallife: Equations help you find unknowns, like how many ₹20 rides you can take at a mela with ₹150 after paying a ₹30 entry fee.

games.title: Solve step by step
games.prompt: Put the steps for solving 3(x − 2) = 2x + 4 in order

quiz.q: Solve 5x − 7 = 2x + 8. What is x?
quiz.mistake: Stops at 3x = 15 and gives 15

quiz.q: Solve 3(x − 2) = 2x + 4. What is x?
quiz.explain: Expand: 3x − 6 = 2x + 4. Then 3x − 2x = 4 + 6, so x = 10. Check: 3 × 8 = 24 and 20 + 4 = 24.
quiz.mistake: Writes 3x − 2 instead of 3x − 6 when expanding

quiz.q: Solve x/3 + 4 = 10. What is x?
quiz.explain: Subtract 4: x/3 = 6. Multiply by 3: x = 18.
quiz.mistake: Divides 6 by 3 instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Meena is 3 times as old as her brother. Together their ages add up to 32 years. How old is her brother?
quiz.explain: Let the brother be x. Then x + 3x = 32, so 4x = 32 and x = 8. Meena is 24.
quiz.mistake: Gives Meena's age (24) instead of her brother's

quiz.q: The sum of three consecutive numbers is 87. What is the smallest of them?
quiz.mistake: Divides 87 by 3 and gives the middle number (29)

quiz.q: Riya has ₹50 more than Arjun. Together they have ₹290. How much does Arjun have?
quiz.explain: Let Arjun have x. Then x + (x + 50) = 290, so 2x = 240 and x = ₹120. Riya has ₹170.
quiz.mistake: Splits ₹290 equally (₹145) or gives Riya's amount

quiz.q: The length of a rectangle is 4 cm more than its width. Its perimeter is 48 cm. What is the width?
quiz.explain: Perimeter = 2(w + w + 4) = 4w + 8 = 48. So 4w = 40 and w = 10 cm. The length is 14 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses w + (w + 4) = 48, forgetting that a perimeter has two lengths and two widths

quiz.q: Solve (2x + 1)/3 = (x + 4)/2. What is x?
quiz.explain: Multiply both sides by 6: 2(2x + 1) = 3(x + 4). So 4x + 2 = 3x + 12, and x = 10. Check: 21/3 = 7 and 14/2 = 7.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies only one term on each side by the LCM

teach.ask: Gappu asks: How do I solve 2x + 3 = 11? Help!
teach.praise: Take 3 from both sides to get 2x = 8, then divide both sides by 2: x = 4. Balanced and solved!
teach.nudge: What can you do to both sides to get rid of the + 3? And then?

learn.hook: Many fields near rivers and many window panes are trapezium-shaped. How can a farmer find the area of a field that is not a neat rectangle?
points: Area of a trapezium = ½ × (sum of the parallel sides) × height, or ½ × (a + b) × h.
The height is the perpendicular distance between the two parallel sides, not the slanting side.
Why it works: two copies of the trapezium, one turned upside down, fit together to make a parallelogram with base (a + b) and height h. Our trapezium is half of it.
Another way: a diagonal splits the trapezium into two triangles with areas ½ × a × h and ½ × b × h.
Remember: parallelogram = base × height, triangle = ½ × base × height. Area is measured in square units like cm² and m².

example.q: A trapezium has parallel sides 10 cm and 6 cm. The distance between them is 5 cm. Find its area.

learn.reallife: Farmers, architects and painters use the trapezium formula for fields, roof panels, staircase sides and window glass.

quiz.q: A trapezium has parallel sides 10 cm and 6 cm, and the distance between them is 5 cm. What is its area?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ (gets 80 cm²)

quiz.q: A field is a trapezium with parallel sides 30 m and 50 m and a height of 20 m. What is its area?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve, or adds all the lengths

quiz.q: A trapezium has an area of 60 cm² and a height of 6 cm. One parallel side is 8 cm. How long is the other parallel side?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ in the formula (gets 2 cm), or stops at 8 + b = 20

quiz.q: Why is the area of a trapezium ½ × (a + b) × h?
options: Two copies fit together to make a parallelogram with base (a + b) and height h
A trapezium is always half of a square
Its parallel sides a and b are always equal
quiz.explain: Turn a copy upside down and join it to the first. You get a parallelogram of area (a + b) × h, and one trapezium is half of it.
quiz.mistake: Memorises the formula without the picture behind it

quiz.q: A trapezium-shaped window has parallel sides 1.2 m and 0.8 m, and a height of 1 m. What is its area?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the parallel sides (1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96) instead of adding them

quiz.q: Which length is the 'height' of a trapezium?
options: The length of a slanting side
The perpendicular distance between the parallel sides
quiz.explain: The height must be measured at right angles to the parallel sides. A slanting side is longer than the height.
quiz.mistake: Uses a slanting side as the height

quiz.q: A parallelogram has a base of 14 cm and a height of 9 cm. What is its area?
quiz.explain: Area of a parallelogram = base × height = 14 × 9 = 126 cm².
quiz.mistake: Uses ½ as for a triangle (63), or finds the perimeter (46)

quiz.q: Joseph's trapezium has parallel sides 9 cm and 15 cm, and a height of 8 cm. He splits it with a diagonal into two triangles. What is the total area?
quiz.explain: Triangle 1: ½ × 9 × 8 = 36. Triangle 2: ½ × 15 × 8 = 60. Total 96 cm², the same as ½ × (9 + 15) × 8.
quiz.mistake: Finds only one triangle, or forgets the ½

teach.ask: Gappu asks: How do I find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 7 and 5 and height 4?
teach.praise: Add the parallel sides (12), multiply by the height (48), then halve: 24 square units. Wonderful!
teach.nudge: Which two sides do you add? What do you do with the height, and is there a half?

topics.title: Area of rhombuses, quadrilaterals and polygons

learn.hook: A rangoli rhombus, a kite for Uttarayan and a hexagonal tile: all can be measured using their diagonals or by cutting them into triangles!
points: Area of a rhombus = ½ × d₁ × d₂, where d₁ and d₂ are the diagonals. This works because the diagonals are perpendicular.
A kite also has perpendicular diagonals, so its area is ½ × d₁ × d₂ too.
Any quadrilateral: take a diagonal d and the perpendiculars h₁ and h₂ to it from the other two corners. Area = ½ × d × (h₁ + h₂).
A rhombus is a parallelogram, so its area is also base × height.
Any polygon can be split into triangles, rectangles and trapeziums. Find each area and add.

example.q: A rhombus has diagonals 10 cm and 8 cm. Find its area.

learn.reallife: Surveyors find the area of oddly shaped plots by splitting them into triangles along a long diagonal.

items.text: A rhombus with diagonals 6 cm and 4 cm has an area of ___
A quadrilateral with diagonal 10 cm and perpendiculars 3 cm and 5 cm has an area of ___
The area of a kite is ½ × d₁ × ___
From its centre, a regular hexagon can be split into ___ equal triangles

games.title: Area truths
items: The area of a rhombus is half the product of its diagonals.
The diagonals are perpendicular, so the area is ½ × d₁ × d₂.
Every rhombus with side 5 cm has an area of 25 cm².
Only the square one does. A leaning rhombus with side 5 cm has a smaller height, so less area.
Any polygon can be split into triangles to find its area.
Joining one corner to the others cuts a polygon into triangles.
A square with a diagonal of 10 cm has an area of 50 cm².
A square is a rhombus: ½ × 10 × 10 = 50.
The area of a quadrilateral is d × (h₁ + h₂).
It is half of that: ½ × d × (h₁ + h₂).
A rhombus is a parallelogram, so its area is also base × height.
Both formulas give the same area.

quiz.q: A rhombus has diagonals 10 cm and 8 cm. What is its area?
quiz.explain: Area = ½ × 10 × 8 = 40 cm².
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ (gets 80) or adds the diagonals

quiz.q: In quadrilateral ABCD, diagonal AC = 12 cm. The perpendiculars from B and D to AC are 4 cm and 6 cm. What is the area of ABCD?
quiz.explain: Area = ½ × d × (h₁ + h₂) = ½ × 12 × 10 = 60 cm². It is two triangles: 24 + 36.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ (gets 120 cm²)

quiz.q: A rhombus has an area of 96 cm² and one diagonal of 16 cm. How long is the other diagonal?
quiz.explain: ½ × 16 × d = 96, so 8d = 96 and d = 12 cm.
quiz.mistake: Divides 96 by 16 and forgets the ½ (gets 6)

quiz.q: A square has a diagonal of 6 cm. What is its area?
quiz.explain: A square is a rhombus with equal diagonals: ½ × 6 × 6 = 18 cm².
quiz.mistake: Treats the diagonal as the side (gets 36 cm²)

quiz.q: Aisha's rangoli is a regular hexagon split into 6 equal triangles, each with an area of 15 cm². What is the area of the hexagon?
quiz.explain: 6 triangles × 15 cm² = 90 cm².
quiz.mistake: Adds 6 and 15 instead of multiplying

quiz.q: A pentagon is split into a rectangle of area 48 cm² and a triangle of area 12 cm². What is the area of the pentagon?
quiz.explain: The parts do not overlap, so add them: 48 + 12 = 60 cm².
quiz.mistake: Subtracts or multiplies the parts

quiz.q: Kabir's paper kite has diagonals of 30 cm and 20 cm. What is its area?
quiz.explain: The diagonals of a kite are perpendicular, so area = ½ × 30 × 20 = 300 cm².
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ (gets 600 cm²)

quiz.q: A rhombus has a side of 13 cm and a height of 10 cm. What is its area?
quiz.explain: A rhombus is a parallelogram, so area = base × height = 13 × 10 = 130 cm².
quiz.mistake: Squares the side (169) as if it were a square, or finds the perimeter (52)

teach.ask: Gappu asks: How can I find the area of a rhombus if I only know its two diagonals?
teach.praise: Multiply the diagonals and take half: ½ × d₁ × d₂. A rhombus is easy now!
teach.nudge: What do you do with the two diagonals? Is the answer the whole product or part of it?

learn.hook: Your school wants a 2 m path around its garden. How much area will the path cover? Cut, add and subtract shapes to find out!
points: A composite shape is made of simpler shapes. Split it into rectangles, triangles or trapeziums and add their areas.
Or start with a big shape and subtract the missing part: area left = big area − cut-out area.
Path outside a rectangle: path area = outer rectangle − inner rectangle. A path of width w adds 2w to the length and to the breadth.
Two paths crossing in the middle: add the two strips and subtract the small square where they overlap, so it is not counted twice.
Put all lengths in the same unit before working out areas.

example.q: A garden is 20 m × 15 m. A path 2 m wide runs all around it on the outside. Find the area of the path.
steps: Outer rectangle: (20 + 4) m × (15 + 4) m = 24 m × 19 m = 456 m²

learn.reallife: Tile shops, painters and gardeners use composite areas to work out how many tiles, how much paint or how much grass seed to buy.

items.q: 10 × 10 square with a 4 × 4 square cut out
Two 1 m crossing paths on a 10 × 6 lawn. Path area?
9 × 4 rectangle with a 2 × 2 square cut out

games.title: Composite checks
items: To find the area of a path around a garden, subtract the garden's area from the outer area.
Outer area − inner area = path area.
A 1 m path outside a 10 m × 8 m garden makes the outer size 11 m × 9 m.
The path is on both sides, so the outer size is 12 m × 10 m.
When two crossing paths are added as strips, the middle square is counted twice.
Before adding areas, all lengths should be in the same unit.
Mixing cm and m gives wrong answers.
An L-shape can be split into two rectangles.
Draw one line to separate the two arms.
The area of any composite shape is its perimeter × 2.
Area and perimeter measure different things.

quiz.q: An L-shaped room is made of a 6 m × 4 m rectangle and a 3 m × 2 m rectangle. What is its total area?
quiz.mistake: Finds only the bigger rectangle, or multiplies the two areas

quiz.q: A garden 20 m × 15 m has a path 2 m wide all around it on the outside. What is the area of the path?
quiz.explain: Outer rectangle = 24 × 19 = 456 m². Garden = 300 m². Path = 456 − 300 = 156 m².
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the garden's perimeter by the width (140), missing the four corner squares

quiz.q: A 10 m × 6 m lawn has two paths, each 1 m wide, crossing in the middle and parallel to the sides. What is the total area of the paths?
quiz.explain: Strips: 10 × 1 = 10 and 6 × 1 = 6. The 1 m × 1 m centre is in both, so 10 + 6 − 1 = 15 m².
quiz.mistake: Counts the middle square twice (gets 16)

quiz.q: A square tile 30 cm × 30 cm has a 10 cm × 10 cm square cut out of the middle. What area is left?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the side lengths first: (30 − 10)² = 400

quiz.q: The front of a hut is a rectangle 8 m wide and 5 m tall, with a triangular roof of base 8 m and height 3 m on top. What is the total area?
quiz.explain: Rectangle = 8 × 5 = 40. Triangle = ½ × 8 × 3 = 12. Total = 52 m².
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ for the triangle (gets 64)

quiz.q: A photo 12 cm × 8 cm has a frame 1 cm wide around it on the outside. What is the area of the frame?
quiz.explain: Outer size = 14 cm × 10 cm = 140 cm². Photo = 96 cm². Frame = 140 − 96 = 44 cm².
quiz.mistake: Uses perimeter × width (40), missing the corners

quiz.q: A floor 5 m × 4 m is to be covered with square tiles of side 50 cm. How many tiles are needed?
quiz.explain: Each tile is 0.5 m × 0.5 m = 0.25 m². Floor = 20 m². 20 ÷ 0.25 = 80 tiles. (Or 10 tiles along by 8 tiles across.)
quiz.mistake: Divides 20 m² by 0.5 m instead of by the tile's area (gets 40)

quiz.q: A trapezium-shaped flower bed has parallel sides 6 m and 10 m and a height of 4 m. A 2 m × 2 m square fountain sits inside it. What area is left for flowers?
quiz.explain: Trapezium = ½ × (6 + 10) × 4 = 32 m². Fountain = 4 m². Flowers = 32 − 4 = 28 m².
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract the fountain, or forgets the ½

teach.ask: Gappu asks: A garden has a path all around it. How do I find just the path's area?
teach.praise: Find the big outer rectangle, subtract the inner garden, and what is left is the path. Smart!
teach.nudge: Which two rectangles can you see? What do you do with their areas?
